newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran conservatives signal trouble for Khatami.
newsitem.headline: Iran conservatives signal trouble for Khatami.

text.p: Conservatives in the Iranian parliament, whose speaker was heavily defeated in the Islamic republic's presidential election, on Wednesday signalled a tough time for ministers in President-elect Mohammad Khatami's cabinet.
Despite feverish speculation and long lists in newspapers of ministerial hopefuls, Khatami has declined to name anyone being considered for cabinet jobs.
Sources close to the Shi'ite Moslem clergyman say he has identified three nominees for every portfolio.

Khatami, a moderate who is backed by Western-style liberals and radical Islamists, was elected in May by a landslide that buried the man confidently tipped to take over, conservative parliament Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri.
Khatami is due to succeed President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani next week.
He must submit his cabinet nominations to the Majlis, or parliament, for approval.

"If Majlis deputies are consulted on the new cabinet before the ministers are officially introduced, certainly the Majlis will act in a more organised and ripe way in giving a vote of confidence," said Ali Akbar Hosseini, a focal figure of the parliament's conservative majority.
Tehran-based analysts said that message, relayed through the official news agency IRNA, was a clear warning to Khatami from the conservatives.

"Since this faction expected to win the presidential elections and had already prepared a list of its ministers...a shadow cabinet is bound to be born for the first time in Iran," Akhbar daily newspaper said.

Another Majlis deputy, Mohammad Shahi Arablou, said in remarks published by Iran News daily that the "secrecy of the cabinet selection process adopted by the president-elect could create problems for the members of the Majlis".
He said that if deputies were not given enough time to investigate proposed cabinet ministers "the number of abstention votes will increase, I'm sure of that".
Conservative Shi'ite Moslem clerics have not minced words in demanding a say over the choice of ministers, analysts said.

In a television debate on Tuesday one of Khatami's most outspoken critics, conservative deputy and editor of Resalat daily Mortaza Nabavi, said the new president should allow a number of ministers from the losing faction into his cabinet "even though they do not agree with his plans in every detail".

Iran Daily said Khatami, who won the election on the back of large numbers of votes by disaffected youths and women, would appoint two new vice-presidents to deal with youth and culture, and women's affairs.
The daily Jomhuri Eslami on Wednesday expressed dismay at Tehran press reports that Iran's ambassador to the United Nations, Kamal Kharrazi, would succeed Ali Akbar Velayati as foreign minister.
It cast doubt on Kharrazi's ability to embark on "absolutely essential" fundamental changes.

"The foreign ministry is in dire need of a thorough spring cleaning. This task can be accomplished by someone who enjoys revolutionary decisiveness away from any political consideration," the newspaper said.
